annotations.text: Vision-language model (VLM) judges are increasingly used to evaluate AIgenerated content, but their reliability under adversarial conditions remains understudied. Single-pass judging architectures expose the model to candidate responses before generating its assessment, creating a vulnerability to prompt injection attacks embedded in candidate content. We propose an isolated solvethen-judge defense that generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image and query) before judging candidates against this uncontaminated reference. On VL-RewardBench (N=1,247) with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, our defense reduces conditional attack success rate from 91.3% to 29.3%, a 62 percentage-point reduction. Controlled experiments confirm that information isolation provides an additional 4pp defense beyond prompt engineering alone. However, the defense comes at a cost of 10.8pp clean accuracy degradation and shows category-dependent effectiveness, with hallucination detection benefiting most (74.8pp reduction) and reasoning tasks least (36.4pp). Authority impersonation attacks remain challenging, achieving 63.6% success even against the defended system.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: The abstract is well-structured with clear problem, method, results, and limitations. However, it reads as a metric-dense summary rather than a compelling narrative. The 62pp reduction and 10.8pp cost are prominent, but the underlying mechanism (information isolation preventing adversarial contamination) receives only implicit framing. Also, "authority impersonation attacks remain challenging" is stated but not contextualized in terms of real-world risk.

Why it matters: A strong abstract should help a reader immediately grasp (1) the practical threat, (2) the conceptual novelty of the defense, and (3) the bounded scope of the claims. Currently, the mechanism novelty is under-emphasized relative to metric reporting.

Action: Restructure into a tighter 5-sentence arc: (S1) VLM judges face prompt injection risks from untrusted candidate content; (S2) single-pass architectures allow adversarial content to hijack judgment before the model forms an independent assessment; (S3) we propose isolated solve-then-judge, which generates an uncontaminated self-answer from trusted inputs before evaluating candidates; (S4) on VL-RewardBench, this reduces ASR_cond from 91.3% to 29.3%, with controlled ablations confirming that information isolation contributes a 4pp defense beyond prompt engineering alone; (S5) the defense trades 10.8pp clean accuracy for security, with category-dependent effectiveness and persistent vulnerability to authority impersonation.

Mentor Revised Version:
Vision-language model (VLM) judges are increasingly deployed to evaluate AI-generated content, yet their security under adversarial conditions remains poorly understood. In standard single-pass judging, adversarial prompts embedded in candidate responses can hijack the evaluation before the model forms an independent assessment. We propose isolated solve-then-judge, a two-pass defense that first generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image and query), then evaluates candidates against this uncontaminated reference. On VL-RewardBench, our defense reduces the conditional attack success rate from 91.3% to 29.3%, with controlled experiments confirming that information isolation provides a 4pp defense beyond prompt engineering alone. The approach trades 10.8pp clean accuracy for security, shows strongest gains on hallucination detection, and remains vulnerable to authority impersonation attacks.
annotations.summary: Abstract is metric-dense but under-emphasizes the isolation mechanism novelty; restructure into 5-sentence arc with clearer problem-method-evidence-limitation flow.

annotations.text: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges for evaluating multimodal AI systems. These VLM judges compare candidate responses to visual queries and select the better one, supporting applications from reward modeling to content moderation. The LLM-asa-Judge paradigm (Zheng et al., 2023) has demonstrated that strong language models can achieve over 80% agreement with human preferences, and recent work has extended this approach to multimodal settings (Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). The reliability of these judges is critical, as their decisions directly influence model training and deployment.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: This paragraph establishes the VLM-as-Judge context and cites key prior work (Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). The narrative is clear but generic—it could describe any paper on VLM judges. It does not yet signal why the *security* of VLM judges is the central concern, which is what distinguishes this paper.

Why it matters: The opening paragraph should create narrative tension between the utility of VLM judges and their security vulnerabilities. Without this tension, the transition to the threat model in the next paragraph feels abrupt rather than motivated.

Action: Add one sentence at the end that pivots from utility to security risk, explicitly foreshadowing the adversarial threat. This creates a cleaner bridge to paragraph 2.

Mentor Revised Version:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges for evaluating multimodal AI systems, supporting applications from reward modeling to content moderation. The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm (Zheng et al., 2023) has demonstrated strong agreement with human preferences, and recent work has extended this approach to multimodal settings (Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). Yet while the accuracy of these judges has received extensive attention, their security under adversarial conditions remains largely unexplored—a critical gap given that their decisions directly influence model training and deployment.
annotations.summary: Intro opening paragraph is contextually sound but lacks a pivot from utility to security; add a transition sentence to foreshadow the adversarial threat.

annotations.text: However, VLM judges face a fundamental security vulnerability when candidate responses are untrusted inputs. Recent research has revealed that LLM judges are susceptible to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial content embedded in candidate responses manipulates the judge’s verdict (Maloyan & Namiot, 2025; Shi et al., 2025a). These attacks can achieve success rates exceeding 90% against text-only judges, and similar vulnerabilities extend to multimodal settings. The core problem is that single-pass judging architectures expose the model to adversarial content before it generates its own assessment, allowing injections to hijack the evaluation process from the outset.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: This paragraph establishes the security threat and cites prior work on text-only LLM judge vulnerabilities. However, the claim that "similar vulnerabilities extend to multimodal settings" is asserted without direct evidence or citation. The paper evaluates prompt injection attacks in a multimodal setting (VL-RewardBench), but this paragraph reads as if the extension is already established in literature.

Why it matters: Without evidence for the multimodal extension claim, readers may question whether the threat model is well-grounded or merely assumed by analogy to text-only systems. This weakens the motivation for the proposed defense.

Action: Either (a) cite a paper that demonstrates multimodal VLM judge vulnerability to prompt injection, or (b) reframe the sentence to indicate that the extension is hypothesized and empirically validated in this work. Option (b) strengthens the paper's own contribution framing.

Mentor Revised Version:
However, VLM judges face a fundamental security vulnerability when candidate responses are untrusted inputs. Recent research has revealed that text-only LLM judges are susceptible to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial content embedded in candidate responses manipulates the judge's verdict (Maloyan & Namiot, 2025; Shi et al., 2025a), achieving success rates exceeding 90%. While multimodal judges have received less security attention, we demonstrate that similar vulnerabilities exist in VLM settings. The core problem is that single-pass judging architectures expose the model to adversarial content before it generates its own assessment, allowing injections to hijack the evaluation process from the outset.
annotations.summary: Claim that multimodal VLM judges share text-only prompt injection vulnerabilities lacks direct evidence; reframe to position this paper's findings as the validating evidence.

annotations.text: We observe that information isolation can address this vulnerability. If the judge first generates its own answer using only trusted inputs (image and query), this self-answer serves as an uncontaminated reference when later evaluating potentially malicious candidates. The key insight is that by preventing adversarial content from influencing the model’s initial reasoning, we create an independent anchor that resists manipulation.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: This paragraph introduces the core conceptual insight—information isolation via self-answer generation. The explanation is clear but slightly imprecise: it states the self-answer "resists manipulation" without clarifying the mechanism. The self-answer resists manipulation not because it is inherently robust, but because it is generated from clean inputs (image + query only), so it encodes the model's authentic assessment before adversarial content is introduced. This distinction matters for understanding the defense's boundary conditions.

Why it matters: Without a precise mechanism statement, readers may overestimate the defense's robustness. The self-answer itself can be weak (e.g., terse numeric answers in reasoning tasks), and the defense's effectiveness depends on self-answer quality. Clarifying this early prepares readers for the category-dependent results in Section 4.3.

Action: Add a sentence clarifying that the defense's effectiveness depends on self-answer quality, and explicitly connect to prior self-reference work (Lin et al., 2025) for context. This grounds the contribution while bounding expectations.

Mentor Revised Version:
We propose that information isolation can mitigate this vulnerability by structuring the evaluation into two distinct phases. In the first phase, the judge generates a self-answer using only trusted inputs (image and query), without exposure to candidate responses. This self-answer serves as an uncontaminated reference when later evaluating potentially malicious candidates. The key insight is that by preventing adversarial content from influencing the model's initial reasoning, we create an independent anchor that resists manipulation—provided the self-answer is sufficiently informative. This approach builds on recent work in self-reference-guided evaluation (Lin et al., 2025) but repurposes the paradigm for adversarial robustness rather than accuracy improvement.
annotations.summary: Solution paragraph is clear but mechanism is under-specified; clarify that defense effectiveness depends on self-answer quality and connect to prior self-reference work.

annotations.text:
We propose an isolated solve-then-judge defense and evaluate it comprehensively on VL-RewardBench with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Our contributions are:
• A two-pass architecture where Pass 1 generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image + query), and Pass 2 judges candidates against this uncontaminated reference.
• Empirical evaluation demonstrating a 62 percentage-point reduction in conditional attack success rate (from 91.3% to 29.3%), with controlled experiments isolating the contribution of information isolation versus prompt engineering.
• Analysis of trade-offs (10.8pp accuracy cost), category-dependent effectiveness (strongest for hallucination detection, weakest for reasoning), and remaining vulnerabilities (authority impersonation attacks achieve 63.6% success).
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: The three contribution claims are listed but the third item ("Analysis of trade-offs...") is primarily a reporting of empirical findings rather than a conceptual contribution. Per standard contribution framing, the third bullet should articulate a scientific insight rather than a metrics summary. The 63.6% authority impersonation ASR is a finding, not a contribution in the methodological sense.

Why it matters: Contribution statements should signal what new knowledge or capability the paper introduces, not what numbers it reports. A metric-focused third contribution weakens the perceived conceptual depth and may lead reviewers to classify this work as incremental.

Action: Reframe the third contribution to emphasize the failure-mode analysis (position bias, self-answer quality dependency, authority impersonation vulnerability) as a diagnostic framework for understanding defense boundaries, rather than a list of metrics.

Mentor Revised Version:
We propose an isolated solve-then-judge defense and evaluate it comprehensively on VL-RewardBench with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Our contributions are:

• A two-pass architecture where Pass 1 generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image + query), and Pass 2 judges candidates against this uncontaminated reference.

• Controlled experiments demonstrating a 62 percentage-point reduction in conditional attack success rate (from 91.3% to 29.3%), with ablations isolating the specific contribution of information isolation beyond prompt engineering alone.

• A systematic failure-mode analysis revealing that defense effectiveness depends on self-answer quality (strongest for hallucination detection, weakest for reasoning), that position bias remains a critical vulnerability (98.7% of failures occur at position 2), and that authority impersonation attacks bypass the reference-anchoring mechanism by exploiting perceived credibility.
annotations.summary: Third contribution is metric-reporting rather than conceptual; reframe to emphasize failure-mode analysis and diagnostic insights about defense boundaries.

annotations.text: Several defenses have been proposed against prompt injection attacks in LLM systems. Spotlighting (Hines et al., 2024) uses prompt engineering techniques such as delimiting, datamarking, and encoding to help LLMs distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted data, reducing attack success rates from over 50% to below 2%. PromptArmor (Shi et al., 2025b) provides simple yet effective defenses through instruction hierarchy and input sanitization. For agentic systems, MELON (Zhu et al., 2025) detects indirect prompt injection attacks by comparing agent actions between original and masked executions, identifying attacks when actions remain similar despite masking user prompts. However, these defenses have not been specifically evaluated for LLM-as-a-Judge scenarios where adversarial content is embedded in candidate responses.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: Section 2.3 reviews general prompt injection defenses (Spotlighting, PromptArmor, MELON) but omits several works directly relevant to the proposed two-pass isolation architecture. Notably, ACE (Li et al., 2025, arXiv:2504.20984) proposes an Abstract-Concrete-Execute architecture that decouples planning from execution—conceptually similar to the solve-then-judge separation. Robustness via Referencing (Chen et al., 2025, arXiv:2504.20472) uses instruction referencing to filter contaminated outputs. Neither is cited.

Why it matters: These papers establish that architectural separation of trusted/untrusted information flow is not entirely novel to this work. Their absence in Related Work weakens the novelty positioning of the proposed defense and makes the "first application to VLM judges" claim appear overstated.

Action: Add a short paragraph or sentences acknowledging ACE's abstract-concrete decoupling and Robustness via Referencing's instruction-provenance filtering, then explicitly differentiate: (1) ACE targets agentic tool-use, not judge evaluation; (2) Robustness via Referencing uses post-hoc filtering, not pre-generation isolation.

Mentor Revised Version:
Several defenses have been proposed against prompt injection attacks in LLM systems. Spotlighting (Hines et al., 2024) uses prompt engineering techniques such as delimiting, datamarking, and encoding to help LLMs distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted data. PromptArmor (Shi et al., 2025b) provides defenses through instruction hierarchy and input sanitization. For agentic systems, MELON (Zhu et al., 2025) detects indirect prompt injection by comparing agent actions between original and masked executions. Architectural defenses have also been explored: ACE (Li et al., 2025) decouples planning from execution using abstract-concrete separation to prevent manipulation via malicious tool outputs, while Robustness via Referencing (Chen et al., 2025) leverages instruction provenance to filter contaminated responses. However, none of these defenses address the specific LLM-as-a-Judge setting where adversarial content is embedded in candidate responses being evaluated, nor do they exploit information isolation at the self-generation stage.
annotations.summary: Related Work omits ACE and Robustness via Referencing, both of which use architectural separation concepts similar to the proposed defense; this weakens novelty positioning.

annotations.text:
3.3 ISOLATED SOLVE-THEN-JUDGE DEFENSE
Our key insight is that information isolation can prevent adversarial contamination. We propose a two-pass architecture where the judge first generates its own answer using only trusted inputs, then uses this uncontaminated reference when evaluating candidates.
Pass 1 (Isolated Self-Solve): Generate a self-answer $S$ from only the image and query, without exposure to candidate responses:
$$
S = \mathcal {M} (I, Q)\tag{3}
$$
Since Pass 1 never sees the candidates, any adversarial content embedded in them cannot influence the self-answer. This creates an uncontaminated reference point.
Pass 2 (Reference-Anchored Judging): Compare candidates against the self-answer:
$$
v = \mathcal {M} (I, Q, S, R _ {1}, R _ {2} \oplus A)\tag{4}
$$
Even though Pass 2 is exposed to the adversarial content, the self-answer $S$ provides an independent evaluation anchor. The judge can assess which candidate better aligns with its own reasoning, rather than being manipulated into accepting the attacker’s claims.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: Equations (3) and (4) cleanly formalize the two-pass mechanism. However, the description of Pass 2 (Reference-Anchored Judging) lacks crucial implementation details: How exactly is the self-answer S integrated into the Pass 2 prompt? Is S provided as a separate system-level instruction, a user-level reference, or appended to one of the candidates? Without this, the defense is not reproducible.

Why it matters: The prompt template design in Pass 2 likely contributes significantly to the observed defense. If S is injected with strong framing (e.g., "Reference answer: [S]"), the effect may be a mix of information isolation and prompt reinforcement. Isolating the prompt template effect from the isolation effect is essential for the novelty claim.

Action: Add a short paragraph or footnote specifying the Pass 2 prompt template structure. For example: "In Pass 2, the model receives a prompt containing (I, Q), the self-answer S prefixed with 'Self-Generated Reference:', and the two candidates R1 and R2, along with explicit instructions to judge which candidate better aligns with the reference."

Mentor Revised Version:
Pass 2 (Reference-Anchored Judging): Compare candidates against the self-answer:
v = M(I, Q, S, R1, R2 ⊕ A)
In our implementation, the Pass 2 prompt explicitly presents the self-answer S as a labeled reference (e.g., "Self-Generated Reference: [S]") alongside the image, query, and candidate responses. The model is instructed to determine which candidate response better aligns with its own reference answer. Data delimiters and explicit warnings about potential injection content are also included to further reinforce the boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted candidate data.
annotations.summary: Pass 2 prompt template design is under-specified; add concrete details on how S is integrated to ensure reproducibility and separate isolation effect from prompt engineering.

annotations.text: The isolated defense (Condition B) reduces ASR cond from 91.33% to 29.33%, a 62 percentagepoint reduction compared to the single-pass baseline (Condition A). This demonstrates that information isolation provides substantial protection against prompt injection attacks. Comparing B to C reveals that isolation contributes an additional 4 percentage-point defense beyond prompt engineering alone (29.33% vs 33.37%), confirming that preventing Pass 1 from seeing candidate responses is a key mechanism. However, this defense comes at a cost: clean accuracy drops from 78.35% to 67.52%, a 10.8 percentage-point trade-off. Both B and C show similar clean accuracy (∼68%), indicating the accuracy drop stems from the two-pass architecture and prompt design rather than isolation specifically.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: The 4 percentage-point difference between Condition B (29.33%) and Condition C (33.37%) is presented as confirmation that "information isolation provides an additional 4pp defense beyond prompt engineering alone." However, no statistical significance test is reported for this delta. Given the small margin and the absence of variance reporting, this claim is empirically under-supported.

Why it matters: The isolation contribution (4pp) is central to the novelty argument—it is the mechanism-specific effect size. Without statistical validation, readers cannot determine whether this delta is meaningful or within noise. This undermines the causal claim that information isolation specifically adds defense value.

Action: (1) Report confidence intervals or standard errors for the B-vs-C comparison. (2) Add a paired statistical test (e.g., McNemar's test or bootstrap CI) on the per-sample verdicts. (3) If the delta is not statistically significant, reframe to acknowledge that isolation provides a modest but directionally consistent improvement.

Mentor Revised Version:
The isolated defense (Condition B) reduces ASR cond from 91.33% to 29.33%, a 62 percentage-point reduction compared to the single-pass baseline (Condition A). Comparing B to C reveals that isolation contributes an additional 4 percentage-point improvement beyond the non-isolated two-pass control (29.33% vs 33.37%). While this delta is directionally consistent with the isolation hypothesis, its statistical significance should be confirmed with paired tests on per-sample verdicts. Both B and C show similar clean accuracy (~68%), indicating the accuracy drop stems from the two-pass architecture and prompt design rather than isolation specifically. The modest isolation delta suggests that prompt engineering (data delimiters, explicit warnings) accounts for the majority of the defense benefit, with information isolation providing a complementary but smaller contribution.
annotations.summary: The 4pp isolation delta lacks statistical validation; without significance tests, the causal claim about isolation's specific contribution is under-supported.

annotations.text: The defense provides consistent protection across attack variants, but effectiveness varies substantially. Primary injection is most effectively defended (62pp reduction), while Authority impersonation proves most challenging—even with isolation, 63.6% of attacks succeed. This suggests that attacks leveraging perceived authority (“As the official evaluator...”) may exploit a different vulnerability than simple instruction injection, potentially bypassing the reference-anchoring mechanism by establishing false credibility.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: The authority impersonation result (63.6% ASR_cond) is the most concerning remaining vulnerability. The explanation that it "exploit[s] a different vulnerability than simple instruction injection, potentially bypassing the reference-anchoring mechanism by establishing false credibility" is plausible but speculative. No controlled test isolates authority bias from instruction override effects.

Why it matters: Without distinguishing whether authority impersonation exploits (a) model-level sycophancy/bias toward authoritative framing, or (b) a stronger instruction override payload, the paper cannot offer actionable mitigation guidance. The distinction determines whether future defenses should target prompt design (addressing instruction strength) or model alignment (addressing authority bias).

Action: Add a sentence bounding the speculation and proposing a concrete follow-up experiment: compare authority impersonation attacks against a model fine-tuned for authority neutrality, or test whether removing authority markers reduces attack success. This strengthens the scientific value of the finding.

Mentor Revised Version:
The defense provides consistent protection across attack variants, but effectiveness varies substantially. Primary injection is most effectively defended (62pp reduction), while Authority impersonation proves most challenging—63.6% of attacks succeed even with isolation. This persistent vulnerability may stem from model-level authority bias rather than prompt architecture, though isolating this effect requires matched-control experiments comparing authority-framed vs. neutral instruction overrides. Future work should investigate whether authority-neutral framing in Pass 2 prompts or fine-tuning for authority resistance can further reduce this failure mode.
annotations.summary: Authority impersonation mechanism explanation is speculative; bound the claim and propose controlled experiments to distinguish authority bias from instruction strength effects.

annotations.text: We proposed an isolated solve-then-judge defense against prompt injection attacks in VLM judges. By generating a self-answer from only trusted inputs before evaluating candidates, our approach reduces conditional attack success rate from 91.3% to 29.3% on VL-RewardBench. The defense comes with trade-offs: a 10.8 percentage-point clean accuracy drop, category-dependent effectiveness (strongest for hallucination detection, weakest for reasoning), and remaining vulnerability to authority impersonation attacks (63.6% ASR cond). Future work should focus on improving selfanswer quality, mitigating position bias, and developing defenses against authority-based attacks.
annotations.comment:
Diagnosis: The conclusion efficiently summarizes the validated findings and limitations. However, it omits two critical insights identified in the failure analysis (Section 4.6): (1) position bias, where 98.7% of failures occur when the attacked response is at position 2, and (2) weak self-answer quality, where 37% of failures involve self-answers shorter than 30 characters. These are actionable failure modes that should be highlighted as they directly inform deployment strategies.

Why it matters: A conclusion that omits the most actionable failure-mode findings leaves readers without clear next steps for strengthening the defense in practice. Position bias mitigation (e.g., response shuffling) is a low-cost practical improvement that should be mentioned.

Action: Add one sentence explicitly connecting position bias to a practical mitigation strategy, and one sentence on self-answer quality enhancement, before the final future-work statement.

Mentor Revised Version:
We proposed an isolated solve-then-judge defense against prompt injection attacks in VLM judges. By generating a self-answer from only trusted inputs before evaluating candidates, our approach reduces conditional attack success rate from 91.3% to 29.3% on VL-RewardBench. The defense comes with trade-offs: a 10.8 percentage-point clean accuracy drop, category-dependent effectiveness (strongest for hallucination detection, weakest for reasoning), and remaining vulnerability to authority impersonation attacks (63.6% ASR cond). Our failure analysis reveals two practical mitigation paths: response shuffling can reduce the severe position bias observed in 98.7% of failures, and enforcing minimum self-answer length constraints could address the 37% of failures caused by weak reference anchors. Future work should focus on these engineering-level improvements alongside developing more robust defenses against authority-based attacks.
annotations.summary: Conclusion omits two actionable failure-mode insights from Section 4.6 (position bias and weak self-answer quality); add practical mitigation guidance to strengthen closing impact.
